User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Schwab. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Thanks — this is a great set of details. I’ll summarize what you can and can’t deduct, recommend whether to itemize, explain the home-office choices (with quick math), list the forms you’ll need, and flag a few clarifying questions that could change the result.

Quick summary / headline recommendations
- You should report your freelance income on Schedule C and will owe self-employment (SE) tax (Schedule SE). The home-office deduction and your $540 business expenses belong on Schedule C.
- The charitable gift ($1,500) is only deductible if you itemize. With the information you gave, your itemized deductions are much smaller than the standard deduction, so you will almost certainly take the standard deduction.
- The student-loan interest deduction has a $2,500 maximum and phases out at modest incomes; based on the numbers you gave, you’re likely above the phaseout and won’t be able to claim it — but see the clarifying question below about when that interest was paid.
- For the home office, the actual method (using your rent share) looks more favorable than the simplified method for your numbers — but the actual method requires a bit more documentation and Form 8829.

What to deduct and where
- Freelance income ($18,400)
  - Report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business).
  - Deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses on Schedule C — this includes:
    - Home-office deduction (either simplified or actual method; see below).
    - The $540 you listed if those were business/unreimbursed expenses for the freelance work. (If those $540 are employee unreimbursed expenses related only to your W-2 job, they are NOT deductible under current law.)
  - After Schedule C net profit is calculated, you’ll also calculate SE tax on Schedule SE (approx. 15.3% on ~92.35% of net self-employment income). One half of your SE tax is an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 (reduces AGI).

- Home-office deduction (self-employed only)
  - You said the office is 120 sq ft exclusive out of a 720 sq ft home → business % = 120/720 = 1/6 = 16.6667%.
  - Two methods:
    1) Simplified: $5 per square foot up to 300 sq ft = 120 × $5 = $600. No Form 8829 required; enter on Schedule C.
    2) Actual: allocate actual home expenses by your business percentage. From rent alone: 16.6667% × $21,000 (rent) = $3,500. You can also include the business share of utilities, renter’s insurance, etc. Actual method uses Form 8829 (Business Use of Your Home).
  - For your numbers, the actual method (just counting rent) gives $3,500 vs $600 simplified — actual looks better. If you have utilities/insurance you can add their pro rata share and increase the deduction. Keep receipts and records.

- Interest income ($2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Schwab)
  - Total interest $2,520 — report on Form 1040. Because total interest > $1,500, you will need Schedule B (Interest and Ordinary Dividends).
  - Expect 1099-INT or 1099-INT/1099-DIV from those institutions.

- Charitable contributions ($1,500 to Salvation Army)
  - Deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). You stated you have a receipt — keep it.
  - With the rest of your facts, itemized deductions will be far below the single standard deduction, so you’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction instead of itemizing, and this $1,500 won’t reduce your tax unless you have other itemizable amounts.

- Student loan interest ($3,200 — Nelnet, 2018–2021)
  - Important clarification needed: the student loan interest deduction applies to interest paid in the tax year for which you are filing. If the $3,200 was paid in 2018–2021 (past years), it is not deductible on your 2024 return. If you actually paid $3,200 of interest in 2024, then:
    - The maximum deduction is $2,500 (above-the-line on Schedule 1) and it phases out for higher MAGI. Based on the income numbers you provided (W-2 + net self-employment + interest), your MAGI is very likely above the phaseout range, so you probably can’t take the student interest deduction — but I can calculate precisely if you confirm whether the $3,200 is 2024 interest or earlier years.
  - You should have a Form 1098-E from your loan servicer for any interest paid in 2024.

Other items to note
- Unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job are not deductible under current law (suspended through 2025 for most employees).
- You may be eligible for the QBI (20% qualified business income) deduction on part of your Schedule C net income — if your taxable income is below the threshold you’ll use Form 8995 (simplified) to claim it. With the size of your business income, you likely qualify for some QBI deduction — I can estimate that if you want.
- You should check whether clients issued 1099-NEC forms for payments >$600; regardless, you must report all income.

Forms you’ll likely need (federal)
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 (Additional Income and Adjustments) — for adjustments like half of SE tax and possible student loan interest (if eligible).
- Schedule B — because your interest income exceeds $1,500.
- Schedule C — to report freelance revenue and business expenses, and to claim home-office deduction (if simplified) or list business expenses (if actual, you’ll compute home-office on Form 8829).
- Schedule SE — to compute self-employment tax and the deductible half-SE adjustment.
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual method for business use of home.
- Form 8995 (or 8995-A) — for QBI deduction (most likely 8995 if your taxable income is below the threshold).
- Keep any 1099-INT, 1099-NEC, W-2, 1098-E, and charitable receipts.

Estimated numbers (quick comparison — actual vs simplified home-office)
- Option A — Actual home-office (rent share only):
  - Business % = 16.6667%; home-office deduction from rent = $3,500.
  - Business expenses total = $3,500 + $540 = $4,040.
  - Net self-employment income = $18,400 − $4,040 = $14,360.
  - Estimated SE tax ≈ $2,029 → half-SE deductible ≈ $1,015.
  - AGI ≈ W-2 (96,500) + net SE (14,360) + interest (2,520) − half-SE (1,015) ≈ $112,365.

- Option B — Simplified method:
  - Home-office = $600 + $540 other business expenses = $1,140.
  - Net self-employment income = $18,400 − $1,140 = $17,260.
  - Estimated SE tax ≈ $2,438 → half-SE deductible ≈ $1,219.
  - AGI ≈ 96,500 + 17,260 + 2,520 − 1,219 ≈ $115,061.

Conclusion from those estimates:
- The actual method lowers your AGI more (by roughly $2,700 in my example) and therefore is likely better for you — at least if you have no other deductions to offset.
- Even with the actual method, your AGI is well above the usual student-loan-interest phaseout ceilings; you likely cannot claim that deduction.
- Your itemizable deductions (as reported) are much lower than the standard deduction, so take the standard deduction.

Clarifying questions that could change the result
1. Was the $3,200 in student loan interest paid in 2024 (the year you’re filing) or in earlier years? If it was paid earlier, it cannot be deducted on your 2024 return.
2. Are the $540 unreimbursed expenses business expenses for your freelance work? (If they are related to your freelance work, they are deductible on Schedule C. If they’re unreimbursed employee expenses for your W-2 job, they’re not deductible.)
3. Do you pay utilities, renter’s insurance, or other home expenses separately (and can you estimate those for the year)? If so, the actual home-office deduction will increase (beyond the rent share).
4. Do you want me to run a full estimated tax calculation (taxable income, federal income tax, SE tax, and an estimate of total tax due) using the actual home-office method so you can see the difference?

If you’d like, I can:
- Re-run the numbers precisely for you (showing taxable income, SE tax, estimated federal income tax, and how much you’d owe or get refunded), but I’ll need answers to Q1–Q3 above.
- Prepare a checklist of records and forms you should gather (1099s, W-2, 1098-E, charity receipts, rent/utility bills).
- Draft an organizer of line-by-line inputs you can use or give to a tax preparer.

Which next step would you like? I recommend first confirming whether the $3,200 student-loan interest was paid in 2024 and whether the $540 is business-related; I can then produce the exact calculations and show the tax difference between simplified vs actual home-office and between itemizing vs standard deduction.
